blocks.x: CSM 177 · Computer Appreciation · Topic 10

Before a presentation is delivered, it needs to be reviewed and rehearsed. PowerPoint offers four view modes for checking your work, printing options for handouts, and animation/transition tools for making slides engaging without becoming distracting.

4slide view modes — Normal, Slide Sorter, Slide Show, and Reading View 6default handout slides per printed page (adjustable to 3, 4, 9, etc.) 4animation categories: Entrance, Emphasis, Exit, and Motion Paths
By the end of this module, you will be able to…

items: 1Identify and use the slide view modes — Normal View, Slide Sorter View, and Slide Show View — and know when each is the right tool for reviewing or rehearsing a presentation.
2Print slides correctly using Backstage Print Preview — choosing a printer, a print range, and a layout (Slides, Handouts, Notes Pages, or Outline).
3Apply, change, and remove animation effects on text and objects using the Animations tab, and preview and reorder those effects.
4Distinguish animations from transitions, apply a transition to one slide or to all slides, and control how slides advance — manually or automatically after a set time.

blocks.x: Key definitions
Slide view A mode of displaying a presentation in PowerPoint that suits a particular task — editing, reordering, or rehearsing. PowerPoint's main view modes are Normal, Slide Sorter, and Slide Show.
Animation Movement applied to text or an object within a single slide — for example, a bullet point flying in or a picture fading into view. Animation happens inside a slide.
Transition Movement that happens as the presentation moves from one slide to the next during Slide Show View — for example, one slide dissolving into the next. Transition happens between slides.
Backstage view The File tab's full-screen menu for tasks that happen outside the slide canvas — including Print, where you choose settings and preview exactly how your printed slides will look.
Slide Views→ Printing Slides→ Animations→ Transitions & Slide Timing
Reviewing your work
PowerPoint provides several ways of looking at a presentation. Each view is designed for a different task — building slides, checking the overall flow, or rehearsing the live delivery.
Normal View

Normal View The default view that opens when you start or open a presentation. The main, center pane is where you create and edit the content of a single slide. A narrow Slides tab runs down the left side of the window, showing small thumbnails of every slide in order — you can click a thumbnail to jump to that slide, or drag thumbnails up and down to reorder the slides.
Slide Sorter View

Slide Sorter View Displays miniature thumbnails of all the slides arranged in a grid across the screen, rather than one slide at a time. Slides can be reordered by dragging and dropping a thumbnail to a new position. Because you can see the whole presentation at once, this view is especially good for confirming that you have all the slides you need, in the right order, before moving on to rehearsal or printing.
Slide Show View

Slide Show View Displays the presentation full-screen, exactly as the audience will see it, with no PowerPoint menus, panes, or editing tools visible. It is used to rehearse or actually deliver a presentation.

Navigating in Slide Show View Move to the next slide or animation step with the Right Arrow key, Page Down, the spacebar, or Enter. Move to the previous slide with the Left Arrow key or Page Up. Press Esc at any time to end the slide show and return to the previous view.
Comparing the view modes

c: Normal View
Create and edit slide content one slide at a time; Slides tab lists all slides
Everyday building and editing of a presentation
Slide Sorter View
Shows miniature thumbnails of every slide arranged on screen; drag-and-drop reordering
Confirming the deck is complete and slides are in the right order
Slide Show View
Full-screen display exactly as the audience sees it; no editing tools shown
Rehearsing or delivering the presentation live

sections.title: What you can configure before printing

blocks.x: From screen to paper
PowerPoint's Backstage Print settings let you preview exactly how a presentation will print before you send it to a printer, and choose the layout that best fits your purpose.

Opening Print settings Click the File tab to open Backstage view, then choose Print. This opens the Print Preview and Settings screen, which shows a live preview of the printed page on the right and all print controls on the left.
What you can configure before printing

items: 1Printer — select which installed printer to send the job to.
2Settings — choose paper size, and whether to print single-sided or double-sided (duplex).
3Print range — choose Print All Slides, Print Selection (only the slides currently selected), Print Current Slide, or a Custom Range (e.g. slides 2–5).
4Copies — set the number of copies to print.

blocks.x: Print layout options

c: Slides
One full slide per printed page
Best when slides themselves are the takeaway document
Handouts
Multiple small slide thumbnails per page for the audience
Defaults to 6 slides per page; adjustable to fewer (e.g. 3, with lines for notes) or more per page; can be arranged horizontally or vertically
Notes Pages
One slide per page with the speaker notes printed below it
Only useful if speaker notes have actually been added to the slides
Outline
The text content of all slides as a plain text outline, no graphics
Good for a quick text-only review of the presentation's structure

blocks.x: Handout details The 3 Slides handout layout is popular because it leaves ruled space beside each thumbnail for the audience to write notes. You can also choose Frame Slides (draw a border around each slide), and toggle between Color, Grayscale, and Pure Black and White to save ink/toner.

items: Confirm the correct printer is selected.
Choose the print range that matches what you actually need (all slides vs. a custom range).
Pick a layout that matches the purpose — Slides for full-page copies, Handouts for the audience, Notes Pages for the presenter, Outline for a text summary.
Check the live preview pane before committing to a large print job.
Set the number of copies and confirm color vs. grayscale before printing.

blocks.x: Movement within a slide
Animation controls how and when text, pictures, shapes, and clip art appear, move, or disappear on a single slide — used to draw attention to key points and improve readability.

Why animate? Animation is used to draw the audience's attention to a specific piece of text or an object at the right moment, and to improve readability by revealing information gradually instead of all at once. Animation can be applied to text, clip art, shapes, and pictures.
Applying an animation effect
Select the object→ Open Animations tab→ Choose an effect from the gallery→ Live preview plays automatically

items: 1Click the text box, picture, shape, or clip art you want to animate to select it.
2Go to the Animations tab on the Ribbon.
3Choose an animation from the gallery of effects; PowerPoint plays a live preview on the slide as soon as it is applied, so you can see the effect immediately.

blocks.x: Applying a different animation effect
To choose an effect outside the default gallery, use the Add Animation button on the Animations tab. Effects are organized into four categories:

items: EEntrance — how an object first appears on the slide (e.g. Fade, Fly In, Wipe).
MEmphasis — draws attention to an object already on the slide, without it entering or leaving (e.g. Pulse, Spin, Grow/Shrink).
XExit — how an object leaves the slide (e.g. Fade Out, Fly Out, Disappear).
PMotion Path — makes an object travel along a specified path (straight line, curve, or custom-drawn path) across the slide.

blocks.x: Removing, previewing, and reordering animations
Removing an animation effect On the Animations tab, open the effect's dropdown and select None to remove that animation from the selected object.

Previewing animations Click the Preview button on the Animations tab to watch all of a slide's animations play in Normal View, or click the Slide Show button to preview them full-screen exactly as the audience will see them (press Esc to return to the editing view).

Reordering animation effects When a slide has more than one animated object, open the Custom Animation task pane and use the up/down arrows at the bottom of the pane to change the order in which the effects play.

sections.title: To one slide, or to all slides

blocks.x: Movement between slides
A transition is the movement that happens as the show moves from one slide to the next. It is applied and controlled through the Transitions tab, alongside settings for how and when a slide advances.

Animation vs. Transition Animation is movement of text or objects within a single slide. A transition is movement that occurs between two slides in Slide Show View — for example, the current slide fading out as the next slide fades in. They are configured on different tabs and serve different purposes, though both add visual interest to a presentation.
To one slide, or to all slides

items: 1Applying a transition to one slide: select the slide, go to the Transitions tab, and look at the Transition to This Slide group — it shows No Transition by default. Click the More dropdown arrow to open the full gallery, and hovering over an effect plays a live preview on the slide before you select it.
2Applying a transition to all slides: choose an effect as above, then click Apply To All so every slide in the presentation uses the same transition.

3Removing transitions: select None in the Transition to This Slide group to remove the transition from just that slide, or select None and click Apply To All to clear transitions from every slide in the presentation.

blocks.x: The star / "Play Animations" icon A small star icon appears beneath any slide that has a transition or animation applied — visible next to the thumbnail in the Slides tab (Normal View) and in Slide Sorter View. Clicking the star plays a preview of that slide's transition and animations without starting the full slide show.
Manual clicks vs. automatic timing
Default: advance on click By default, slides advance when the presenter clicks the mouse (or presses Enter) during Slide Show View, giving the presenter full control over pacing.

Automatic timed advancement On the Transitions tab, in the Advance Slide section, check Automatically After and enter a time (in seconds/minutes). The slide will then advance on its own after that interval, without a click. This is especially useful for unattended presentations, such as a looping display running at a trade show or kiosk with no presenter clicking through it.

Setting timing per slide Slide advance timing can be set individually for each slide in the Advance Slide section, or entered once in Slide Sorter View and applied uniformly with the Apply to All option so every slide in the deck advances after the same interval.

blocks.title: Summary — Transitions tab at a glance

items: Transition to This Slide group: gallery of transition effects, defaulting to No Transition.
Apply To All: copies the current slide's transition (or its removal) to every slide.
Advance Slide: On Mouse Click (default, manual) and/or Automatically After (timed, automatic) — both can be checked together.
Star icon under a slide thumbnail signals it has a transition and/or animation, and can be clicked to preview it.
